title: perf-bench-scratch-maya-lopez-2026-02-27
content:
Perf bench scratchpad - Redwood serving runtime
Author: Maya Lopez (notes)
Date range: 2026-02-24 -> 2026-02-27
Purpose: quick experiments to compare latency/throughput across batching, KV-cache, and quantization settings for model: rwkv-7b-like (internal alias: rwl-7b-v1).

---
Experiment matrix (short):
- Model: rwl-7b-v1 (fp16), rwl-7b-q4 (4-bit quantized)
- Hardware: p4d-ish cluster (A100 equiv), single-GPU per worker for these runs
- Sequence lengths: 128, 512, 1024 (tokens)
- Batch sizes tested: 1, 4, 8, 16
- KV-cache: enabled/disabled (enabled = reusing prefix caches across requests)
- Batching mode: dynamic (continuous batching) with 20ms collection window
- Metrics captured: tokens/s (throughput), p50/p95/p99 latency (ms), GPU util (%), memory (GB)

Raw summarized results (select highlights)
Format: seq | batch | kv | model | tokens/s | p50(ms) | p95(ms) | p99(ms) | note
128  | 1   | off | fp16 | 420   | 18   | 45   | 120  | cold KV, low batch -> low tokens/s
128  | 8   | off | fp16 | 2800  | 85   | 220  | 520  | batching increases throughput, latency worsens for tail
128  | 8   | on  | fp16 | 5200  | 40   | 110  | 300  | KV-cache doubles throughput for short seqs
512  | 1   | off | fp16 | 120   | 45   | 110  | 290  | single request large seq -> high latency
512  | 8   | on  | fp16 | 900   | 260  | 540  | 980  | batching helps tokens/s but p99 high (spikes)
1024 | 4   | on  | fp16 | 350   | 380  | 820  | 1500 | large seq p99 very spiky
128  | 8   | on  | q4   | 7600  | 50   | 130  | 350  | q4 improves tokens/s ~1.45x vs fp16 in these runs

Quick ASCII chart (tokens/s by batch @ seq=128, kv on, model fp16):
batch: 1  4   8    16
tps  : 420 1400 5200 6200
bar  : █    ███  ██████████  ██████████████
(note: bars are illustrative)

Observations / hypotheses:
1) KV-cache is the single biggest win for workloads with prefix reuse. For seq=128 it roughly doubles tokens/s and reduces median latency. Tail p99 still problematic under mixed batches.
2) Batching increases throughput linearly-ish up to GPU memory limits but hurts p99 latency (higher variance, queuing effects). For user-facing low-latency routes we need smaller windows or latency SLO-aware routing.
3) Quantization (q4) gives ~1.4x-1.8x throughput improvement with modest latency impact; quality evals are needed but initial small-sample comparisons look acceptable for retrieval-augmented generation prompts.
4) Large sequences (>=512) show high p99 spikes even at modest batch sizes; likely kernel-execution fragmentation + memory thrash. Need to profile kernel timelines.
5) GPU utilization is low for batch=1 runs (~30-45%) suggesting CPU-side slowdown or inefficient kernel batching. For batch>4 utilization climbs to 70-90%.

Anomalies / notes: 
- Run at 2026-02-25 15:23 had an outlier p99 3x normal for seq=512/batch=8/kv=on. Correlated with a background job (checkpoint sync) in node logs. Need to re-run with clean nodes.
- Observed sudden 10-15% lower throughput on node gnode-12 for q4 runs; GPU clocks were lower (power cap triggered). Filed INF-789 to track scheduler/power behavior.

Micro-profiling TODOs:
- Collect nvprof-like traces for seq=1024/batch=4 to identify kernel hotspots and NVLINK stalls
- Add timeline traces (server side) to correlate request arrival -> queueing -> gpu-op -> response
- Test smaller batching window (5ms) vs 20ms to quantify tail latency tradeoff
- Try dynamic padding heuristics (per-batch max-seq) to reduce wasted compute for mixed-length batches

Quick next experiments (priority order):
1) Re-run seq=512/batch=8/kv=on on isolated node (no background sync) to validate p99 anomaly (high)
2) Run q4 vs fp16 for a larger eval set (200 prompts) to measure quality deltas (BLEU/ROUGE-like + human spot check)
3) Implement 5ms window A/B and measure p95/p99 changes for low-latency route
4) Collect 10 nvprof traces across runs for kernel ordering analysis

Notes for follow-up PRs / tickets:
- GH PR: performance/tuning: change default batching window to 10ms for low-latency routes (draft PR exists: https://github.com/redwood-inference/rex/pull/1234)
- JIRA: INF-789 tracking node-level throughput variance (filed 2026-02-26)
- Confluence: add these runs to Perf Dashboard (page link above) for team visibility

Short conclusions (working):
- For PLG-hosted API with mixed traffic: default should be kv-cache enabled + adaptive windowing. Quantization as opt-in for non-sensitive workloads.
- For Dedicated (SLA) tiers: allow customer control of batching window and latency vs cost tradeoff; expose expected p99 vs throughput curves per model+config in Console.
